newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China plays in HK likely to see more downside.
newsitem.headline: China plays in HK likely to see more downside.

text.p: China plays on the Hong Kong stock market will feel downward pressure in line with mainland bourses in the next two weeks after Beijing cracked down on state banks trading in shares, analysts said on Wednesday.
"H-shares might be affected but there shouldn't be too great an impact on red chips," said Charles Cheung, executive director at J & A Securities.
H-share companies would be harder hit because they fall within the sphere of the ban, analysts said.
"The circular issued by the government specifically targets state enterprises," said economist Shawn Xu at Merrill Lynch.

H-shares are Hong Kong-listed shares in China-incorporated enterprises, many of which also have shares listed in Shanghai or Shenzhen. Red chips are Hong Kong-incorporated and listed companies with Chinese financial backing.
Last Thursday, the People's Bank of China ordered all Chinese banks to unwind their stock market positions within 10 days from the receipt of its seven-point directive.
The directive also banned all margin financing by stock brokers and forbade state enterprises from using borrowed funds to invest in mainland stock markets.
"The measures are the most serious action taken so far to cool speculation in China," said Merrill's Xu.
The action follows evidence that many Chinese enterprises were found to have taken out working capital loans but put the money into the stock market, said Xu.
State enterprises, including listed companies, have been actively playing the markets, he added.
H share Tianjin Bohai Chemical Industries (Group) Co revealed a profit of 18 million yuan from share trading in its 1996 annual report.
But the company said it halted the activities in September, following an earlier People's Bank of China crackdown on speculation in the stock market.

Analysts said the moves by the central bank should be seen as a forerunner to measures to be taken by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) to control speculation in red chips after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
"We believe measures to control red chips have been postponed until after the July handover," said Sunny Chan, senior research manager at Seapower Securities. "This is just a prelude to that action."
The CSRC and the National Administration of State Property may seek to tighten controls over asset injections by Chinese parent companies into Hong Kong red chip subsidiaries, analysts said.

The Hong Kong market is also waiting to see how well, or how poorly, the territory's own securities watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission, and Beijing's CSRC cooperate and how they divide responsibilities, they said.
Analysts generally view the current action as positive.

"With investigations (of 30 banks and brokers in China) under way and new personnel in charge of the exchanges, also less cash flowing into the markets, it is very likely the indices will fall further," said Merrill's Xu.
"But this is good for the health of the market," he added.
On Tuesday, Yamaichi Securities' red chip index fell 84 points, or three percent, to 2,819. It is 5.1 percent off its high of 2,962 set on June 4.
The Hang Seng China Enterprise Index of H-shares fell 23.09 points, or 2.19 percent, to 1,032.47 on Tuesday, compared with the blue chip Hang Seng Index's 1.47 percent fall.
